introduction-limiting-the-blast-radius.core: Blast radius is how much of your system and customer base a single failure can affect. You can't prevent all failures, but you can bound their impact with isolation: AZs and regions, cells, shuffle sharding, and statically stable designs that don't need changes to survive.

first_principles.problem: A single bad config push takes down every customer at once.

analogy.title: Fire doors in a building
analogy.story: A fire is contained to one section instead of spreading through every floor.
analogy.breaks: Fires spread physically; software failures spread through shared code, config and dependencies.

example.title: Measuring impact
flow: After: push per cell, 1 of 20 first → 5% max

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Bad change caught at small scale.

check.a: The scope of systems and customers affected by a single failure.

cell-based-architecture-the-ultimate-bul.core: Cells are complete, independent copies of a service stack (compute, data, queues) serving a partition of customers, with a thin routing layer mapping customer → cell. Cells have a fixed maximum size, so scaling adds cells, and failures, overloads or bad deploys stay within one cell.

first_principles.problem: A shared database overload during one tenant's spike degrades the service for all tenants.
truths: Routing must be minimal and reliable.
derivation: Build a **thin, static router** (mapping table, DNS).

analogy.title: Bulkheads in a submarine
analogy.story: Each compartment has its own air and seals; one flooded compartment doesn't sink the vessel.
analogy.breaks: Submarines have fixed compartments; you add cells as customers grow.

example.title: SaaS cell layout
flow: Each cell: ALB, ECS service, Aurora, SQS
Router: DynamoDB mapping cached at edge

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One noisy tenant affects ~8% at most.

check.q: How does a cell-based system scale?
check.a: By adding more fixed-size cells rather than growing a single shared stack.

shuffle-sharding-the-math-of-resilience.core: Shuffle sharding assigns each customer to a random combination of k workers out of n. A poison customer can only break its own k workers, and the chance another customer shares all k is tiny (1 / C(n,k)). With 8 workers and k=2 there are 28 shards; with 100 workers and k=5, about 75 million.

first_principles.problem: In simple sharding, a bad customer takes down its whole shard and every customer on it.
truths: Clients can retry on other workers in their shard.
Full overlap is what causes shared outage.
derivation: Route53 name servers use this pattern.

analogy.title: Giving each guest a random pair of keys to different doors
analogy.story: If one guest jams their doors, almost nobody else uses exactly the same pair.
analogy.breaks: Guests choose doors; shuffle sharding needs clients that retry across their assigned workers.

example.title: Impact maths
flow: Simple sharding (4 shards of 2): bad customer hurts 25% of customers
Another customer fully overlaps with probability 1/28 ≈ 3.6%

check.q: How many unique shuffle shards exist with 8 workers and 2 per customer?

static-stability-surviving-without-chang.core: A statically stable system rides through failure using resources and state it already has: pre-provisioned capacity in remaining AZs, cached configuration, pre-established connections and data-plane-driven failover. It doesn't need to launch, reconfigure or call control planes while things are breaking.

first_principles.problem: Recovery depends on autoscaling and config updates, both of which are impaired during the incident.
truths: Impairments often affect those same planes.

analogy.title: A ship with full lifeboats already lowered
analogy.story: In an emergency, you step in; nothing needs to be built or ordered.
analogy.breaks: Lifeboats sit unused; idle capacity costs money every hour.

example.title: EC2 in 3 AZs
flow: AZ fails → 6 remain, health checks drop the bad AZ

check.q: Why doesn't static stability rely on autoscaling during an AZ failure?
check.a: Autoscaling uses control-plane APIs and capacity that may be impaired; static stability already has enough capacity running.

putting-it-together-the-isolation-zone-s.core: Layer isolation techniques: regions for disaster recovery, AZs with static stability for facility failures, cells for software and tenant failures, shuffle sharding within cells for noisy or poisonous clients, and progressive deployments across all of them. Each layer catches failures the others don't.

first_principles.problem: Teams apply one isolation technique and assume they're covered.
truths: Each technique addresses specific failure modes.

analogy.title: Russian dolls of protection
analogy.story: Each layer encloses and protects the next.
analogy.breaks: Dolls nest neatly; real architectures have cross-cutting shared services that must be isolated too.

example.title: Deployment waves
flow: Wave 1: one cell in one AZ in one region
Wave 2: rest of that region's cells
Wave 3: other regions, one at a time

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Bad changes caught at minimal blast radius.

check.q: Which isolation layer protects against a single tenant's poison requests?
